title: Private VPC deep dive - networking & runtime performance
summary: Deep technical session covering Private VPC deployment patterns (PrivateLink vs NAT vs VPC peering), subnet design, DNS/Route53 considerations, egress control, and how Redwood runtime optimizes latency and throughput (KV cache, batching, quantization). Action items include benchmark plan, network diagram exchange, and pilot schedule.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-22 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel (Redwood PM); Maya (CTO), Samir (Platform), Ellen (SecOps), Tom (ML)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we have an hour plus — this is Alex from Redwood, I'm the account lead, Priya is our SE, Daniel is product. Quick run of the agenda, dig into networking (PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS) and then runtime perf (latency/throughput, KV cache, batching, quant).
[00:18] Maya: thanks, we really want to understand the network requirements for private VPC — security team is especially focused on egress and DNS visibility.
[00:30] Priya: Great, I'll start with the high-level VPC patterns we typically see: 1) PrivateLink endpoints to our control plane for most customers (keeps everything in carrier, sorry in AWS backbone), 2) S3/VPC endpoints for model artifacts, and 3) optional NAT egress for third-party telemetry.
[00:45] Samir: Can you clarify PrivateLink vs VPC peering? Any perf/latency differences?
[00:56] Priya: Sure, PrivateLink gives you an interface ENI in your subnet and we route to that, it's encrypted and doesn't require routing table changes across accounts; peering is direct L3 routing which can be lower hop count but requires route propagation and cross-account config. In our experience latency delta is small (single-digit ms) but depends on AZ placement. Also PrivateLink helps with fine-grained IAM and security.
[01:20] Ellen: If we use PrivateLink, what about DNS resolution? We need hostnames to resolve to the interface endpoints and to be able to use our internal resolver.
[01:30] Priya: We typically recommend creating private hosted zones or use Route53 resolver inbound/outbound endpoints. For PrivateLink our service name resolves to the interface IPs; you can control via conditional forwarding. We have a doc that shows Route53 resolver endpoints + endpoint security group example.
[01:50] Tom: For runtime, my main fear is noisy-neighbor latency spikes — how does Redwood ensure p99 under a 3s SLA-ish requirement?
[02:02] Daniel: Good question — our runtime uses continuous batching plus prioritized routing. We isolate high-SLA customers into dedicated pools when needed, and we have KV cache warmup strategies — warm cache dramatically reduces token generation latency. For p99 we tune batching window and admission control so a single request doesn't get stuck behind a very large batch.
[02:30] Maya: can you explain KV cache eviction behavior? if we have many concurrent chats will the cache thrash?
[02:42] Priya: The KV cache is per-model-session and we use LRU with size-aware eviction; for very high concurrency we recommend pinning sessions for warm pinning or using dedicated pools. There's also a shared prefix cache option for common prefixes. Typical hit rates depend on prompt reuse; we saw 70-90% hit rates on chatty workloads in our benchmarks.
[03:05] Samir: What about egress for S3 model pulls? We prefer no public internet egress — can models be pulled over VPC endpoints only?
[03:16] Priya: Yes — we support S3 VPC endpoints and you can restrict access via bucket policies and IAM roles for cross-account. For large model weights we support pre-warming and staging in a customer-owned S3 to avoid internet egress.
[03:35] Ellen: Any requirements for NAT Gateway? We run a centralized NAT vs per-subnet.
[03:45] Priya: If you use PrivateLink for control plane and VPC endpoints for artifacts, you may not need NAT for inference nodes. NAT is only required if you need outbound internet access (third-party logging, telemetry). Centralized NAT works but watch throughput limits; NAT gateway has bandwidth and SNAT port constraints which can matter during large model pulls.
[04:05] Tom: switching back to runtime perf — batching: what batch sizes and latency tradeoffs do you see for a 2-token generation baseline?
[04:18] Daniel: For small requests low-seq (<=128 tokens) we default to micro-batching with latency SLOs — typical batch sizes 8-32 depending on concurrency. The runtime adapts batch size based on queue depth and predicted latency targets. For streaming use-cases we have partial-output streaming to reduce perceived latency.
[04:42] Samir: How deterministic is throughput when quantizing to INT8? We worry about quality regressions and throughput gains.
[04:54] Priya: INT8 gives 2-3x throughput improvements on many kernels but quality can vary by model. FP16 is lower-risk with 1.2-1.6x gains. We run model-specific evals and can provide suggestions: quantize-and-compare on a sample eval set. We also support mixed-precision kernels and per-layer fallback for problematic layers.
[05:20] Maya: Are there any network packet-level recommendations for low p99? MTU, TCP keepalive, or keep sockets warm?
[05:30] Priya: Keep MTU standard 1500 unless you explicitly enable jumbo frames; more important is ensuring correct TCP keepalive and connection pooling. We recommend long-lived connections (reuse TLS) via PrivateLink so the handshake cost is amortized. Also ensure ENI placement in same AZ as compute to avoid cross-AZ hops.
[05:50] Alex: Quick interjection — we often see customers accidentally use public DNS which leaks to internet resolvers causing tail anomalies. Ellen: is that something you can control?
[06:00] Ellen: yes we control our resolvers, we just need the specifics of what hostnames to whitelist.
[06:08] Priya: We'll send a list of hostnames and FQDNs (service endpoints and S3/content endpoints) in the reference doc.
[06:20] Tom: Regarding KV cache metrics — do you expose hit-rate, eviction_rate, cache_size per-session?
[06:30] Daniel: Yes our Console exposes token-level breakdowns including cache hits/misses, per-route latency histograms, and batch size distributions. We can surface those at 1-min granularity in Dedicated/Private deployments.
[06:50] Samir: For Private (on-prem) deployments, how does control plane connectivity work? Are we expected to open specific outbound endpoints or is it fully air-gapped option?
[07:02] Priya: We offer both: options for private control plane with direct PrivateLink to your VPC or fully air-gapped on-prem where you run Redwood control plane components locally. For PrivateLink we need specific interface endpoints and port ranges (we'll send). For air-gapped we require installation packages and an ops window.
[07:28] Maya: If we go with PrivateLink + dedicated pools, what's the expected end-to-end tail latency for a chat use-case 256 tokens with streaming? p95/p99?
[07:40] Daniel: With warm KV cache and dedicated pools, p95 often around 150-300ms per response chunk depending on model; p99 can be 2x-3x that without careful tuning — hence we do admission control and batch shaping to keep p99 under target. For very strict p99s we typically recommend dedicated capacity and local model variants tuned for latency (quantized, optimized kernels).
[08:05] Tom: Do you have any empirical numbers for delta between PrivateLink and same-VPC ENI (peering)?
[08:14] Priya: Empirically we've seen between 1-6ms difference depending on AZ mapping. For cross-account peering there's sometimes additional route table traversal. But overall the runtime costs dominate for long responses.
[08:30] Alex: let's talk about test plans — we recommend a staged benchmark: 1) model warmup and cache priming 2) steady-state qps at target concurrency 3) traffic spike test 4) network partition simulation.
[08:42] Maya: For cache priming do you need our conversation history or will synthetic prompts suffice?
[08:50] Tom: synthetic usually fine but for true hit rates we should use production-ish prefixes. We'll share an anonymized set.
[09:00] Priya: Great. On quantization note — we can run an A/B where we test FP16 baseline vs INT8 on your eval set and show token-level quality delta + latency improvement.
[09:15] Samir: Anything on TLS termination — do you terminate at our side or at Redwood? If we use PrivateLink are certs mutual-TLS?
[09:26] Priya: We support mutual TLS for PrivateLink; TLS terminates at the interface endpoint ENI and we authenticate via mTLS or customer-provided certs for advanced setups. For some customers we also provide IAM-based endpoint policies.
[09:46] Ellen: Is there audit logging for requests? We need S3 object access, model pull logs, and per-request metadata for compliance.
[09:56] Daniel: Yes, Private deployments include audit logs, request-level metadata, and optional KMS integration for keys. Logs can be shipped to your S3 or SIEM via secure endpoints.
[10:10] Alex: Samir earlier asked about NAT port exhaustion — big model pulls can open many ephemeral ports; recommended practice?
[10:22] Priya: Use S3 VPC endpoints and pre-stage model artifacts in EBS or local cache to avoid large concurrent pulls. If NAT is required, use multiple NAT gateways or a NAT fleet with autoscaling. Also consider FIP reuse strategies.
[10:40] Tom: In terms of batching heuristics — is it fixed window or dynamic? and can we set latency SLO per route?
[10:50] Daniel: Dynamic. The runtime uses a combination of latency goal (deadline-based) and queue depth prediction. You can set per-route SLOs in the rollout config and the admission controller will enforce them by rejecting or routing to dedicated pools.
[11:10] Maya: Are there network-level metrics we should gather to correlate with p99 spikes?
[11:20] Priya: Collect ENI packet drops, retransmits, TCP RTT, route changes, and resolver latencies. Also track AZ-level capacity — cross-AZ failover can introduce spikes. We'll provide a checklist.
[11:36] Samir: Any gotchas on outbound IP allowlists if we use PrivateLink and a shared Redwood fleet?
[11:45] Priya: With PrivateLink your traffic stays in your VPC to the interface ENI; you won't need outbound IPs for runtime calls. For hosted fallback (if you want Redwood's hosted as backup) we have a known set of IP ranges you can allowlist; we'll include them.
[12:00] Alex: Okay, lets transition to the final recap and next steps.
[12:06] Maya: quick question — what about DNS TTLs? We worry about stale ENI IPs after failover.
[12:14] Priya: Use low TTLs (30-60s) for the service name, and Route53 resolver will repopulate quickly. PrivateLink tends to keep ENIs stable, but low TTL helps during failover.
[12:30] Alex: Recap: Redwood to send reference network diagram, hostnames list, port ranges, and a proposed benchmark plan. Customer to share anonymized prompt set, firewall rules, and a target pilot date. Action items noted.
[12:46] Priya: I'll attach a short checklist for NAT/S3/PrivateLink and the Route53 resolver steps.
[12:55] Maya: thanks all, we'll sync with security and pick a pilot week.
[13:00] Alex: Thanks everyone, I'll follow up with calendar invite for the benchmark window.

Notes: occasional transcription errors present (eg 'K-V cash' instead of 'KV cache', 'carrier' for 'AWS backbone', small mis-attributions).

End of transcript.
